Neonatal Lesser horseshoe bats emerge into a world of complete dependency, their minute bodies weighing just 2.1 grams [Wwb = 2.1 grams] at birth, a value that represents roughly 46 percent of the adult mass they will eventually attain. This modest birth weight is typical of small-bodied insectivorous bats, reflecting the energetic constraints on the gestating female who must carry developing young during an energetically demanding period. The gestation period, measured as 67 days [tg = 67 days] at the typical active body temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C], aligns closely with predictions for a mammal of this body size. This relatively prolonged intrauterine development suggests a strategy of producing a single, relatively well-developed offspring rather than multiple smaller young, a pattern common among rhinolophid bats. The single pup per reproductive event [N_R_i = single pup per reproductive event] is a consistent feature across populations, with females producing just one litter annually [F_R_i = one litter annually]. This conservative reproductive output reflects a life-history strategy oriented toward high offspring survival rather than high fecundity, a trade-off that becomes particularly evident when one considers the species' modest adult body size and the challenges of navigating complex cave environments during foraging.

Weaning represents a critical transitional milestone in the development of young Rhinolophus hipposideros, with pups achieving nutritional independence at 35 days after birth [tx = 35 days after birth] under the controlled thermal conditions of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C]. This relatively brief period of maternal investment, measured from parturition to the cessation of lactation, is notably shorter than the 67-day gestation that precedes it. The rapid transition from milk dependency to independent foraging is energetically demanding for the weanling, which must quickly develop the echolocation skills and flight proficiency necessary to capture aerial insects. By the time of weaning, juveniles have already undergone substantial somatic growth, although they remain considerably smaller than adults. The steady increase in body mass during the nursing period is fueled entirely by the mother's milk, which is exceptionally rich in lipids, allowing the pup to nearly double its birth weight before beginning to consume solid food. The timing of weaning is also closely tied to seasonal peaks in insect abundance, ensuring that newly independent young encounter favourable foraging conditions during their first weeks of solo hunting.

Sexual maturation in the Lesser horseshoe bat proceeds along a sexually dimorphic trajectory, with males reaching reproductive maturity considerably earlier than females. Under the standard thermal conditions of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C], male pups attain puberty at 471 days after birth [tp = 471 days after birth], a developmental schedule that allows them to become reproductively active before completing their second summer. Females, by contrast, require a longer period of somatic growth and fat accumulation before their first ovulation, reaching puberty at 500 days after birth [tp = 500 days after birth] at a temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C]. This approximately one-month delay in female maturation is a common pattern among temperate-zone bats and is thought to reflect the greater energetic demands of gestation and lactation, which impose a premium on achieving a sufficiently large body size and adequate fat reserves before embarking on reproduction. The age at first successful breeding for females thus typically occurs during their second year of life, following their first hibernation period. This delayed reproductive onset, combined with the production of only a single offspring per year, means that even modest rates of adult mortality can have substantial consequences for population persistence.

The ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown adult Lesser horseshoe bats is 4.6 grams [Wwi = 4.6 grams], a remarkably small body mass that places this species among the tiniest of European bats. This diminutive adult size imposes stringent physiological constraints, particularly with respect to thermoregulation and energy balance. Because surface-area-to-volume ratios are high in such small endotherms, maintaining a core body temperature of 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C] during active periods requires a high mass-specific metabolic rate. The 4.6 gram asymptotic mass is achieved after several months of post-weaning growth, during which juveniles gradually acquire the skeletal and muscular development necessary for sustained flight. Adult body mass fluctuates seasonally, with individuals accumulating fat reserves prior to hibernation and then losing substantial mass over the winter months when they rely entirely on stored energy. Females tend to be slightly heavier than males on average, a dimorphism that likely reflects the energetic burdens of pregnancy and lactation. The small body size also permits access to narrow crevices and tight roosting spaces that provide thermal buffering and protection from predators.

Longevity records for Rhinolophus hipposideros indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 22.4 years [am = approximately 22.4 years] under the thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods at 34.8 °C [T = 34.8 °C], an extraordinarily long life for a mammal weighing only 4.6 grams at adulthood. This combination of extreme longevity, small body size, and low annual reproductive output (one pup per year) places the species at the slow end of the mammalian life-history continuum, a position more commonly occupied by larger-bodied species with lower mortality rates. The 22.4 year maximum recorded lifespan far exceeds what would be predicted from body size alone under standard allometric equations, suggesting that other factors such as low predation risk in cave roosts, seasonal torpor reducing accumulated oxidative damage, and a highly effective DNA repair system contribute to extended somatic persistence. Captive individuals have occasionally surpassed this value, although field records confirm that free-living bats routinely survive for more than a decade. The extended reproductive lifespan means that even a female producing only one pup per year can potentially contribute multiple offspring to the population over her lifetime, partially offsetting the constraints imposed by low fecundity.
